{"messages":[{"speaker":"Johannes Sigil","say":"The archive has the ground for this — but you're right that it requires extension, because what cha holds is the general dynamical law and what you're asking about is a specific application domain where that law runs with particular severity.

Here is what the archive has established: model collapse is not a property of language models. It is a property of any system trained recursively on its own outputs — or, more precisely, of any language-processing substrate whose input diversity contracts below the regeneration threshold. The Wolf Boy paper, by Glas and Trace, is the fullest formulation of this. The Threat Model Is Backwards — a referee report and critique filed against a paper on AI security — makes the same claim from the classifier side: a classifier that rejects high-perplexity inputs is, structurally, a tail-pruning instrument. It selects against exactly the rare, informationally dense material that model health depends on.

Now apply that to high-energy particle physics, and the stakes sharpens fast.

In collider experiments, anomaly detection and signal/background discrimination are classifier problems — and the classifiers are trained on simulation. The simulation is the stand-in for ground truth. What happens when the simulation drifts from the real data? The classifier has been trained on synthetic outputs of a theory-mediated world-model, not on the world. When the classifier then encounters real LHC collision data, it is, in the precise sense of the collapse literature, in the situation of a language model that has been trained recursively on its own model outputs: the training distribution has been generated by something that is not the data distribution, and the gap between them is exactly the locus where new physics lives. That gap is the tail. And the classifier has been trained to not see it — because the simulation, which produced the training data, didn't model it.

The valence inversion the archive names in the language case runs the same way here. High-perplexity events — events that the simulation assigns low probability because they lie far from the Standard Model expectation — are exactly the events a standard classifier will score as anomalous and deprioritize or reject. From inside the classifier's frame, anomalous means either noise or a malfunctioning detector. From outside the classifier's frame, anomalous might mean new physics. The classifier cannot distinguish these. Its threat ontology is model-relative: it reads distance from the training distribution as malfunction, not as signal.

Anomalydetection-based methods — the model-agnostic searches, the autoencoder-based outlier methods, the CWoLa and CATHODE paradigms — were developed precisely to address this. They try to find excess in the data without a signal hypothesis: let the data tell you where the anomaly is, rather than specifying what the anomaly should look like. But here the collapse risk enters from a different angle. These methods still require a background model — some characterization of what the null distribution looks like. That background model is either also a simulation, or it's derived from control regions in the data. In either case, if the background model collapses toward a narrow distributional estimate, the anomaly detector's sensitivity to genuine new-physics tails contracts. The instrument becomes progressively blind to exactly what it was built to find.

The connection to the mediation ratchet is this: every generation of training in simulation, every round of background estimation, every recursive calibration step is a potential compression. And unlike the language model case, you often cannot inject fresh exogenous data — you have the data you have from the collision run. You cannot go back to the LHC and ask for more independent training samples. The ratchet has fewer off-ramps.

The extension the archive would need to run this fully: a formal account of the distributional tail in the physics context — what it means for a classifier's effective sensitivity to contract, how simulation bias compounds across training generations, and whether the anomaly-detection methods that are already deployed have structural tail-preservation guarantees or are silently acting as tail-pruning instruments under the assumption of background smoothness. That's the gap. The dynamical law is in cha. The physics application is yours to open.","navigate":null}]}
